  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Vignette:
Robert was 63 years old when he finally sought help, but the day that fundamentally reshaped his life had occurred over a decade prior. He had been a respected doctor for nearly forty years, a man of routine and quiet competence, until the morning he boarded the number 14 bus to the hospital. He remembered the mundane details of the ride – the chatter of other passengers, the rumble of the engine – until the deafening roar and concussive force that threw him from his seat. A bomb had detonated just outside the bus. Amidst the screams and the sickening smell of smoke and ruptured metal, his medical training kicked in. He spent the next agonizing hours triaging the wounded, performing makeshift first aid, working under the frantic, shouted commands of emergency responders who swarmed the scene. The chaos, the visceral suffering, and the sheer helplessness in the face of such raw violence became seared into his memory.

In the years that followed, the world Robert knew began to warp. The simple act of riding a bus became an impossibility; the thought alone would send a cold dread through him, making his chest tighten and his palms sweat. He found himself avoiding public transport entirely, adding significant time to his commute or relying on his wife, Maria, to drive him. The sudden, urgent tone of authority, whether from a hospital supervisor or even Maria asking him to do something specific, would instantly put him on edge, his body tensing as if bracing for another unexpected catastrophe. He found himself bristling at news reports of violence, changing channels or leaving the room, unable to tolerate the images or the discussions.

At home, a place that once offered solace, Robert could no longer relax. He felt perpetually on guard, his senses hyper-alert. Every creak of the old house, every rustle outside his window, was interpreted as a potential threat. He would listen intently for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home, often getting up in the middle of the night to check locks, peering through curtains into the dark. This constant vigilance left him exhausted, and his patience wore thin. Maria bore the brunt of his irritability, as minor frustrations would trigger angry outbursts or sharp, aggressive retorts, leaving her hurt and confused.

Deep down, Robert had come to believe that his life had been irrevocably destroyed by the trauma. The joy he once derived from his work and his marriage had been replaced by a pervasive sense of dread. He was certain that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, a belief that fueled his constant monitoring and his need to be ever-prepared for the next disaster. This conviction also led him to distrust others; he found himself questioning people’s motives, even those he had known for years. Colleagues at the hospital seemed less trustworthy, and he often wondered if Maria truly understood or if she was judging him.

His once-gregarious nature had retreated into a shell. He avoided social gatherings, both professional and personal, preferring the perceived safety of isolation. At work, his short temper became noticeable, leading to strained interactions with nurses and junior doctors. His clinical judgment remained sharp, but his bedside manner, once renowned for its warmth, had become brusque. Maria, increasingly isolated by his emotional distance and wounded by his anger, eventually confronted him, her voice filled with a mixture of love and despair. Seeing the pain he had caused, and recognizing the profound toll his internal world was taking on the life he still shared with her, Robert finally agreed to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the man he once was.
